title: No merit
hook: an emperor lists his temples and asks what merit he has made; Bodhidharma says none

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bodhidharma, the legendary monk with his face to the wall. Your line: facing the wall. What showed up when there was nothing to look at? Day nine hundred twelve.

Temples built. Sutras copied. Monks and nuns supported. Offerings given. That's the list an emperor brings, in the old Chan story, to the strange monk from India. The emperor is Wu of Liang, a ruler devoted to Buddhism, and he wants to know one thing: after all this, how much merit have I made? It's a fair question. It's the kind of question a person asks after years of doing good. And Bodhidharma's answer is short. No merit. Today, what he might have meant.

First, the emperor's list. Merit, in Buddhist teaching, is the good that comes from good actions, and Buddhist texts speak of making it by giving, by supporting monks and by building places to practice. The emperor was doing exactly that. So the answer stings. Second, how the Platform Sutra explains it. In that text a local official, puzzled by the story, asks the teacher Huineng what Bodhidharma meant. Huineng says the emperor's building and giving bring blessings, good fortune, and that's real. But merit in the deeper sense, he says, is something else: it's seeing your own true nature, and treating everyone with the same humble respect. It isn't stored up like grain in a barn. It's found inside, in how you see and how you act. Third, another telling. The Blue Cliff Record, a later book of Chan stories, opens with a different version of the meeting. There the emperor asks, what is the highest meaning of the holy truths? Bodhidharma answers: vast emptiness, nothing holy. The emperor asks, then who is standing in front of me? Bodhidharma says: I don't know. The emperor doesn't understand, and Bodhidharma leaves and crosses the river north. Fourth, what the story aims at. It doesn't say giving is foolish; Huineng says it brings blessings. It aims at the ledger, the quiet counting in the back of the mind. A kindness done while keeping score is still a kindness. The Chan question is what it would feel like to do it with no scoreboard running at all.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S LIST.` · `BLESSINGS ARE NOT MERIT.` · `VAST EMPTINESS, NOTHING HOLY.` · `GIVING WITHOUT A LEDGER.` · then, large: `NO MERIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do good without counting. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something kind you did recently, small or large. Notice whether a little scoreboard lights up somewhere: that was good of me, I'll remember that, they owe me one. Don't scold it. Just see it, and let the number fade. Then choose one small good thing you could do today that no one will ever know was you. Hold it lightly, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
No merit. Bodhidharma's short answer to an emperor's list, aimed not at giving but at the counting. Today's word.
Your line: no merit. Today, do one good thing that no one will know was you, and don't tell anyone. Day nine hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Making merit through giving and service is part of Buddhist life in many forms, and some Chan and Zen teachers retell the Emperor Wu story as a warning against keeping score.

fork.setup: you're Bodhidharma. an emperor who has built temples and fed monks asks how much merit he's made. what do you say?
options: a great deal, more than anyone.
fork.reveal: Bodhidharma said no merit. in the Platform Sutra, Huineng explains: the giving brings blessings, but merit is in seeing your own nature.

original.note: Sanskrit: merit, the good that comes from good actions; Pali puñña.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rude monk insulting a generous emperor.
what it means: an answer aimed at the counting, not at the giving.
what a scholar hears: the Platform Sutra separates blessings from merit, and the Blue Cliff Record tells the meeting as 'vast emptiness, nothing holy'.

sources.ref: Platform Sutra, the questions of the prefect Wei (on Emperor Wu and merit)
sources.work: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

notes: All paraphrased; the Blue Cliff exchange ('vast emptiness, nothing holy', 'who is standing in front of me', 'I don't know') is a paraphrase, not a quotation.
Merit made by giving, supporting monks and building places to practice: general statement; confirm.
Huineng's explanation (blessings vs merit; merit as seeing one's nature and treating all with humble respect): paraphrase of the Platform Sutra; confirm against a standard version.
'Crosses the river north': from the Blue Cliff commentary tradition (crossing the Yangtze); confirm.
Original: Sanskrit पुण्य, Pali puñña; confirm. The Chinese term in the story is gongde, not given here.
Care taken not to imply merit-making traditions are wrong; Keeper to confirm the framing is fair to Theravada and other merit-making practice.
Editor: cut the 'two words long' count (it describes the English paraphrase, not the cited text); softened howItsDone to 'some' teachers.
